question.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)=6{e}^{2t}+2{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}$ for $s>2.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{6{e}^{2t}+2{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}\} \\  & =L\{6{e}^{2t}\}+L\{2{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}\} \\  & =6L\{{e}^{2t}\}+2L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{3}\} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}\} & =\frac{6}{(s+4)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =6L\{{e}^{2t}\}+2L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}\} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{s-2}+2\cdot \frac{6}{(s+4)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{s-2}+\frac{12}{(s+4)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$
